paragraphs.text: The word of God, brothers, as we have often said before, is simple and clear, plain to all and full of abundant light. But since it has different workings, it receives different names, so that it is often called light and life, lamp and torch, sword, river and spring, knife, axe and door. It takes these names according to the benefits it gives, to open the eyes of the hearers' minds and to lead our understanding up from the things around us to the things above us. That is why our Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God, the fountain of wisdom, used parables when he spoke with the people. He taught what is beyond the world through what is in the world, the invisible through the visible, the divine through the human. Sometimes he offers a parable of a vineyard, sometimes a parable of fishing, sometimes of a dragnet, at other times of leaven. So today, speaking to the Jews, he said: "A man had two sons, and he said to the first, 'Go and work in the vineyard.'" These are the things we live among and spend our days with, so he uses them to guide us to the wisdom that is above the world, as he did on the earlier occasion. Yesterday the Savior said: "The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard."

Yesterday he brought in the parable of a vineyard, and today the same. We must also take note of the times at which the master of the vineyard went out. He went out, it says, early in the morning, and about the third hour, and the sixth, and the ninth, and the eleventh. So there are five times of calling: early morning, the third hour, the sixth, the ninth and the eleventh. Nothing is idle with God. He who warns, "You will give an account for every idle word," would much less use an idle word himself, he who is the fountain of wisdom. So the divine school teaches us that God calls at different times. The master is the same, and he has the same farm, but he issues his call at different times to the different generations of mankind. The day is the same, the master the same, the vineyard the same. The times at which he hires are not the same: early morning, the third, the sixth, the ninth, the eleventh. When did he go out early in the morning to hire laborers? By "morning" he means the beginnings of God's creation. It was morning when Adam was formed. At the beginning the world had only just raised up the new sun, and the beauty of the moon and the fair order of the stars had only just been displayed. Early in the morning the master went out to hire. Whom did he hire first among men? Adam. He placed him in paradise to work it and to keep it. So the first period runs from Adam to Noah; this is one call, one time. In that time Adam was hired for work, and Abel for the work of virtue, and Seth, and Enoch, who was taken up because of his surpassing virtue. The first time of calling lasts until Noah. When Noah appeared, at the time of the third hour, he went out again to hire. The first generation had been wiped out for its lawlessness, so the human race again needed a second call. He brings laborers into the vineyard a second time, those from Noah to Abraham: a second call. Pay careful attention, I beg you. The first hour is the period from Adam to Noah; the third hour, from Noah to Abraham; the sixth hour, from Abraham to Moses; the ninth hour, from Moses to Christ; the eleventh hour, from Christ to the consummation. As the eleventh hour is the end of the day, so the time of his coming was the end of the ages. As the eleventh hour hurries the day toward its end, so the time of his coming points to the consummation. That is why the apostle Paul says: "These things, brothers, happened to them as types, and they were written down to instruct us, on whom the ends of the ages have come." And see the wonderful thing: the first were hired, then the second, the third, the fourth, and finally the fifth. Yet the wage was not given to the first until the last arrived. They endured the toil but have not yet received the wage. God did not wish to give the first their wage until the fruits of the Church should arrive and he should command the steward: "Pay them, beginning with the last and ending with the first." Paul testifies in the Epistle to the Hebrews that God put off giving the first their wage until the last should come. He mentions Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the patriarchs, and other prophets and righteous men, and adds: "And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had foreseen something better for us, so that they would not be made perfect apart from us." Here, brothers, he gave five times and five callings. To go over them again: the first time, from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to Moses; the fourth, from Moses to Christ; the fifth, from the Savior to the consummation. In the same way he sets forth a parable elsewhere and says: "The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who went out to meet the bridegroom: five were wise and five were foolish." Why five and five? Because in every generation there are both righteous and unrighteous. Five wise and five foolish: for in every generation there are both the zealous and the lazy, both the devout and the irreverent.

See how the times agree everywhere. These five callings each have their own particular tasks and their own time. Farmers demand from each season the fruits proper to it: from spring what belongs to spring, from winter what belongs to winter, from summer what comes from summer, from autumn what belongs to its own turn of the year. In the same way God, when he demands fruits, demands from each time the fruits proper to its generation. He does not demand of you today the fruit he demanded of the first. After Christ's coming he demands another. He did not demand of those before you the fruits proper to your time, but he demands of each generation its own fruits, and so it was then too. Then it was another time, and it had its own law; now it is another time, and it has its own ordinance. This is not because God has changed, but because he fits his command to the time. That is why Scripture often testifies of Noah: "And Noah was righteous, perfect." How? "In his generation," that is, compared with those who lived alongside him. Each person is required to give the service of his own generation, as Peter says about David: "David, after he had served his own generation, fell asleep by the will of God." Each according to his own generation. So there are five generations. We say these things not as mere assertions of our own, but following in the Master's footsteps. The Savior displayed his power. "Returning to the city," it says, "he saw a fig tree, and it had nothing but leaves, and he was looking for fruit." He came to it hungry. I see great difficulty in these words, unless his power shames our minds out of saying or thinking anything careless about God and makes us follow the aim of the truth. "Returning," it says, "very early, while it was still night, he was hungry, and he came to the fig tree looking for fruit, and did not find any; for it was not the season for figs." So it is written. Now who, I do not say God, and I am not now bringing the dignity of God into the discussion, but what person even among people like us is so senseless and foolish as to go to a fig tree out of season? If he acted as a man, it is not like a sensible person to look for fruit out of season. If he acted as God, why was he ignorant of the limits of his own creation? However you choose to examine the saying, whether by his humanity or by his divinity, it does not seem to fit the Savior. A sensible man does not demand fruit from plants out of season; indeed people would not even think of demanding it in the first place. Nor would God himself, who set order and season and laws for every plant and fruit, have demanded it in breach of his own limits. For if you yourself ordained the proper season for the fig tree, [?] when it did not bear; and if it was the season and it bore no fruit, this came from the will of God, who had not given the plant strength. So, brothers, this is a matter of divine dispensation rather than need. It was not Christ's need but a dispensation: he wished to give his disciples assurance about the passion in advance. Right after this deed he was about to enter Jerusalem and undergo the passion. Anyone who reads carefully will find the power of the cross following on this story. He was about to enter Jerusalem and suffer, and the disciples were going to be scandalized by the passion. So that no one would suspect he suffered from weakness, he gives clear evidence that he could have withered those who opposed him as he withered the fig tree. He shows his power on the lifeless fig tree, and his patience toward rational human beings. With the miracle fresh in their memory, they would realize that he who withers with a word endured willingly.

That this account is true, brothers, and that he arranged all these things to show his power, can be understood from what follows. Many are free to understand and interpret it this way: the fig tree, they say, is the synagogue of the Jews, and he threatened the synagogue, "May no fruit ever come from you again." Some have chosen to interpret it so. But the facts turn out not to agree with the prediction. After the cross, after this sentence, tens of thousands of Jews believed, and that so many believed does not fit "no more fruit from you." Take up the saying again. If he pronounced against the Jews and against the synagogue that it should never again bear fruit, and the churches are the fruits of the synagogue, then after this sentence no Jew should have believed. But hear from Scripture that many did believe. One public speech of Peter's netted three thousand, another of his teachings four thousand, and the souls came to about seven thousand. Elsewhere, as the word advanced, a great crowd of Jews became obedient to the faith. Many Jews obeyed, many thousands, and in the end the word spread so far among the Jews that the apostles said to Paul: "You see, brother, how many tens of thousands of believing Jews there are." If then there are tens of thousands of believing Jews, if tens of thousands believed, how does this agree with the sentence, "May no fruit ever come from you again"? After the sentence, tens of thousands of fruits blossomed. No, the matter follows this sequence. Flee forced allegories. Sometimes Scripture itself gives us eyes for spiritual contemplation; sometimes it teaches us itself to read figuratively. But when what lies before you is plainly either a spiritual meaning or a historical account, do not force what cannot be reached, but take what you hear in its natural order. The cross was at hand; the passion was about to be revealed. So that they would not put the dispensation down to weakness, he shows his power on a lifeless thing and keeps his patience for those who were to have hope of salvation. For the Savior knew that the cross was the salvation of mankind, and that his being lifted up on the wood was what would net the whole world. That is why he says: "If I am lifted up" (that is, if I am crucified) "I will draw all people to myself." Pay attention, I beg you: what does "lifted up" mean? Unless he himself interprets the saying, I cannot pin down its meaning. The Savior says to Nicodemus: "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that whoever believes in him may not perish but have eternal life."

"And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up." What does this riddle mean? Once in the wilderness the Jewish people grumbled about their food, the manna. They trampled on this food given from heaven and longed for an Egyptian table, saying: "We remember the pots of meat we ate in Egypt." The pots of Egypt were preferred to the manna of heaven. What then did God do? Since the bread from heaven had been despised, he sent deadly serpents among the people. Serpents came out, biting and bringing death with their bites. It was fitting that no other beast was sent, not a lion, not a bear, but serpents. From the beginning God had said to the serpent, "You shall eat dust all the days of your life," and so he sent this kind of beast. Against those who ate and grumbled he sent the biting serpent, which eats and does not grumble. Death followed the bites. They fell down before Moses; Moses fell down before God. God provided a remedy for the wounds. Though he could have driven the serpents away when he was entreated, he left the plague and gave the remedy as well: "Make me a bronze serpent and fix it on a pole at the door of the tent of witness, and proclaim to the children of Israel and say: If anyone is bitten by a serpent, let him come and look at this serpent fixed on the pole, and if he believes he will live." Was it not possible to put the serpents to flight? Was it not possible to destroy them? Was it not possible to heal with a word? But the word of God could have brought water out of the rock, and yet the rock did not obey until it saw the sign of the cross. So it is here too. He could have put the serpents to flight, but their bites were not blunted until they saw the image of the cross, which deadens the bites of the demons. But why did he make the serpent an image of the Savior? What do the Savior's image and a serpent have in common? It was so that you may remember how you receive salvation and blessing from the Crucified, when you deal with Jews or with any enemies who take their starting point from Scripture and wage war against Scripture. For it is written: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." Pay close attention. A Jew or some other enemy of the Church may snatch words from Scripture, arm them against Scripture, and say: "How can you want a blessing from the crucified Lord, when Moses plainly writes, 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree'?" Say to him: "If you have read Scripture, understand it." What is required is not reading but understanding, as Philip says to the eunuch: "Do you understand what you are reading?" And what does the well-disposed man reply? "How can I, sir, unless someone guides me?" If he says, "How can you receive a blessing from the Crucified? For it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,'" say to him: "How did the children of Israel in the wilderness receive a blessing from the serpent, when God had said from the beginning, 'Cursed are you above all the beasts of the earth'?" The serpent is cursed, and cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. Do not fix your attention on how the words are arranged, but learn the difference. The Savior was going to take upon himself the curse laid up for the world. The first curse was: "Earth you are, and to earth you shall return." He took this sentence upon himself, as the apostle says: "He redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us." He prefigured this by setting an image in the serpent, and it was fitting that he did so in the serpent. That bronze serpent had the look, form and image of a serpent, but it did not have the serpent's venom and malice. In the same way the Savior appears in the flesh in the outward form of sin. For this flesh had become sinful before he came. So he takes on sinful flesh, not because he sinned himself, but because he took up the sin of the world: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." So the Savior took on flesh that had the true image of flesh but not the sin of flesh: "For he committed no sin," says Isaiah, "nor was deceit found in his mouth." What venom is in a serpent, deceit is in a human being. Of this Scripture says about the wicked: "The venom of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness," and: "With their tongues they have practiced deceit." So, to repeat once more: that serpent had the image and form of a serpent, but not the venom and malice of a serpent. In the same way the body of the Savior had human form, but not human wickedness.

Here is another image. There the serpents that bit were some, and the one that suffered for them was another. It would have been fitting to take one of the biters and crucify it. But the biters were let go, and the one that had done no wrong was crucified. The one that had no share in the corruption or destruction of the other serpents endured being fixed on the pole, because it was an image of the Savior. All human beings had sinned, yet none of the sinners is crucified for the sinner; the sinless one is. You have grasped the spiritual meaning. Remember the Lord's words to Nicodemus: "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that whoever believes in him may not perish but have eternal life." "So must the Son of Man be lifted up": a fine saying. Since the passion was thought to be a humiliation, the Savior calls it an exaltation. The whole world was exalted by the cross; the whole world, lying on the ground, was raised upright through the dispensation of the cross. That is why "the Lord reigned; he clothed himself with majesty… for he set the world aright." He did not say "created." First he created it; second, he set it aright. "So must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that whoever believes in him may not perish." It seems necessary to me to call as a witness to this exaltation a prophet who plainly proclaims that God is exalted. Hear then the blessed Isaiah proclaiming this exaltation. He proclaimed the passion with the greatest clarity when he said: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer; he bears our sins and suffers pain for us; for the sins of my people he went to his death." Yet elsewhere he calls the passion itself an exaltation. What does he say? "Sing hymns to the Lord, praise his name, declare his glory among the nations, for he has done lofty things. Rejoice and be glad, you who dwell in Zion, for the Holy One of Israel has been exalted; in your midst he has been exalted."

But a heretical voice pops up against this and says: "Even if he was exalted, it was the Father who exalted him. For it is written: 'Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven,' and so on." The enemies of the truth always attack the preaching of the truth. With such people it is necessary not to give answers straight away, but first to demand that they account for their own assumptions, and only then to bring in the solution to the questions. You say that the Father highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus, and the rest. First establish for me what this name is that is above every name. It is not enough simply to make a pronouncement; one must stand on the truth. When the wicked ask a question, undo their absurd question with a just question in return. The Savior showed today how to answer the crooked. The Pharisees questioned the Savior, saying: "By what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you this authority?" The Savior wished to show that one must not satisfy wickedness, and must not answer absurd questions. So he says to the Pharisees: "I will ask you one question; if you tell me, I too will answer you. The baptism of John, where did it come from? From heaven or from men?" He who "catches the wise in their own craftiness" shut the wicked in. "By what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you this authority?" When asked, he does not answer them but asks in return: "I too will ask you one question." That is why the prophet says: "With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent, and with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the crooked you will be perverse." Many have thought this saying is spoken by God to men. But the prophet says these things to God: with the righteous you will be righteous, with the innocent man you will be innocent, with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the crooked you will be perverse. So that you may learn that he is speaking to God, he adds: "For you will save a lowly people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud." The Savior always tormented the wickedness of the Jews with his silence, for wickedness that is not satisfied is tormented all the more. He was often questioned and did not answer. The Jews pressed him, and he gave them no reply. He tormented their souls so much that the Jews once said to him: "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly." Still he did not answer, except: "I have told you many times, and you do not listen. Why do you want to hear it again?" See how they themselves proclaimed the torment of their souls: "How long will you keep us in suspense?" "Did you not say, 'Ask and you will receive; knock and it will be opened to you; seek and you will find'?" You have read Scripture, but you have not understood the passage that says, "The wicked will seek me and will not find me." Learn from this that the one who spoke through the Gospels and the one who spoke through the prophets have the same character, and that he himself is the one who spoke through both. Here, when the Jews questioned him, he did not answer but bound them with questions in return. In the same way, in the Old Testament, God says to Ezekiel: "Son of man, see, the sons of the people are coming to me to ask a question. As I live, I will not answer them." Do you see the same character? See how many torments, how many questions, how many demands, and he did not answer. But where he finds a simple soul and faith, full of light and simplicity, he not only satisfies it when he is asked, but teaches it even when he is not asked.

Once Jesus went into the region of Samaria. He found a Samaritan woman drawing water and said to her, "Give me a drink." The giver of life says to her, "Give me a drink." He was sitting by the well, the spring above the spring. Then, to be brief (for my purpose is not to unfold the present story but to come to the subject at hand), she asked [?]. She asked him a question disputed between Jews and Samaritans, since the Samaritans have their place of worship near what is now called Neapolis, while the Jews worship in Jerusalem. The Samaritan woman says to him, "Sir, our fathers worshiped on this mountain; how is it that the Jews say one must worship in Jerusalem?" See a soul eager to learn: a pitiable woman, yet lofty in her strength. She came out to draw water, and she draws streams from the spring. The Samaritans worship here, the Jews in Jerusalem: settle the question. The Savior says, "Truly I tell you, woman, the hour will come when they will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. For God is spirit," that is, everywhere, "and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth," not confining worship to a place, but singing his praise everywhere. Since she could not clearly understand what the Savior was saying (for it went beyond the woman's understanding), the woman says to him, "I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will teach us all things." See a soul that had longing before it had sight. The Jews saw and did not believe; she, though she had not yet seen him, awaits him. When Christ saw her simple mind, he says, "I am he, the one who is speaking to you." How many questions the Jews asked, and how they were tormented! "How long will you keep us in suspense?" And he did not answer. She said in her words, "He is coming," and the one proclaimed revealed himself. This is what is said: "Crooked thoughts separate from God, but he shows himself to those who do not distrust him."

Since, then, the fountain of wisdom has taught us to resolve absurd questions with counter-questions, I ask the heretic: What is this "name that is above every name"? Say it however you like. What is the name? That he is called Jesus? That he is called Christ? That he is called Savior? Tell me the name. First take your stand, so that when I bring forward the divinely inspired testimony, the glory of the prophets, the preaching of the apostles, you will not set the testimony aside. But first establish your meaning. Tell me what name you think is the one above every name. But what am I to do? I am among the faithful, and I do not want to leave the children of the Church hanging on account of the enemies. Let us, then, unfold the matter, and if any enemy is present, let him be benefited and become a friend instead of an enemy, and in agreement instead of opposed. Let him not consider it a defeat to be defeated by the truth. Let him not strive to win the bad victory, but to suffer the good defeat. Let us unfold the argument as they understand it. What name do you say was granted to him, the name above every name? That he was called Jesus? Before him Joshua the son of Nun was called Jesus. That he was called Christ? Every king and prophet is a christ, an anointed one. So David speaks of King Saul: although he was wicked, he nevertheless had the royal anointing. When he was being advised by some of his guards, "Look, this is the day on which the Lord said he would deliver your enemy into your hands; strike him down," David says, "As the Lord lives, I will not lay my hand on him, for he is the Lord's anointed." And not just one anointed, but many: "Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no harm to my prophets." And Habakkuk: "You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones." How, then, is it above every name? For if others had the name before him, how did the Father give him a name above every name, or what name was it? That he was called Savior? Many were called saviors. Remember what was said earlier. What is the name above every name? But since you have no chance to answer, or you know and act in bad faith and hide it on purpose, learn this: Scripture often uses "name" of God to mean not a title but glory. The name of God means the glory of God; for example, when he performs wonders, he gains a name from the wonder, as the blessed prophet says: "Where is he who brought up Moses with his right hand? He overpowered the water before his face, and led his people out in the wilderness, and made himself a name," that is, fame; in other words, you became renowned. We say this of ourselves too: "a man of name," not from having a name (for everyone has a name), but from being named everywhere. He calls "name" the glory and fame that is spoken of everywhere. So God says to Solomon, "And I have made you a name, like the name of the kings of old." Yet he did not change his name; was he not called Solomon? But "I have made you a name" means fame, glory. So here too he says, "He gave him a name," that is, glory. And what is the glory? So that I need not interpret it myself, listen to Paul himself saying: "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord." You see that by "name" he meant glory: the worship of the whole world, his being glorified everywhere and proclaimed throughout the whole world. "Yes," he says, "I accept the interpretation, but I do not retreat from this point: that the Father gave him the name." "Do you want," he says, "to understand the name as a title? Do you want to understand the name as glory? Do you want to call it fame? Renown? For my part I still do not retreat from this: God gave him a name; therefore God also highly exalted him." We must, then, look into this. For the phrase appears to be like a reward given to the Savior. Paul says: "Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name." It is shown here that because he suffered, he received a reward for his suffering. Since he humbled himself unto death, "therefore God also highly exalted him." For "therefore" states the reason for which he bestows glory on him. This glory and exaltation is the reward of the suffering. Who, then, is the one who suffered? Who is the one who received the reward? So that you may not be allowed simply to rage against the Godhead, Paul added: "And he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death; being made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself." Pay close attention. First he spoke of the form of God: "being in the form of God." Then he pointed to the form of a servant: "taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man," in order to show that the form of the servant, the man, is what receives the reward and the name. For there are two. Since the Savior laid down his soul (for he had a soul, since he took on a complete man), the flesh itself, which served the Savior Word, receives as its reward to be honored with the name above every name, and that every knee should bow to Christ, in heaven and on earth and under the earth.

I will mention another point briefly. If he received these things after the cross, and if, because he humbled himself unto death, God rewarded him by giving him a name, if it appears that he did not have this name before the cross, then he received the glory as a favor. Struggle along with me, for the thought is subtle and deep. They say that because Christ suffered (they read the Apostle without understanding the apostolic meaning), because he suffered, therefore God highly exalted him "and granted him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth." Before [?] the cross he received a reward. Now if before the cross the Only-begotten does not appear to be worshiped, and every knee does not appear to bow to the Only-begotten, then truly he received a reward; he received as a favor what he did not have. But if even before the cross, before he suffered and before he was exalted, the Dispensation is found being worshiped by all creation, what room is left for idle talk? Why, wretch, do you not recognize what belongs to the dignity that is before the ages, and what to the form of the dispensation in the flesh? Understand the form of God and the form of a servant, the one assuming and the other assumed. Do not confuse the order; do not obliterate the truth. Or rather, do not be obliterated by the truth.

Let us show, then, whether every knee bows and the Only-begotten is to be worshiped even before the Dispensation, not having received his worship from the cross, but having it both before the cross and before the ages. Listen to what it says. The blessed Isaiah says: "Thus says the Lord: I am the Lord God, and there is no other; a righteous one and a savior, there is none besides me. Turn to me and be saved, all you from the end of the earth. I am God, and there is no other." The same sequence continues: "By myself I swear, surely righteousness shall go forth from my mouth. I am God, there is no other; a righteous one and a savior, there is none besides me." I am God, and again, there is no other. A third time he takes it up and says: "Turn to me; by myself I swear, surely righteousness shall go forth from my mouth. My words shall not be turned back" — that is, my word does not go out in vain — "for to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear by the true God." Every knee, every tongue. Who is the one who said this? The Father. For that is what the heretic wants, not to honor the Father, but to strip the Son of his own glory. But for me, the believer, and for the Church, the Father is understood to have said these things, the Son is understood to be saying them, and the Holy Spirit is proclaimed. This is how they spoke of God, and there is no difference. For he established that "I am righteous, and there is no other."

Who, then, is the one saying these things? Let them be asked that for the moment. But since they are likely to say among themselves, like the Pharisees, "If we say this, he will answer us that," I will let them simply speak, and from this very prophecy I will bring forward Paul as a witness. Let us see Paul and this prophecy, "As I live, by myself I swear, that to me every knee shall bow and every tongue." Let us see where Paul brought it in. He once wrote to the Romans. The believers who had become Christians from among the Jews and from among the Greeks were at odds with one another. Those who had become Christians from among the Greeks partook of all foods without distinction. But those from among the Jews wanted both to worship Christ and to observe the Jewish food laws. Each side reproached the other. Those from the Jews reproached those from the Gentiles for not keeping the law. Those from the Greeks reproached those from the Jews for not walking in line with the grace of the gospel. Those from the Greeks said to the Jews: "If it is the law that justifies, why did Christ come? And if Christ came, why do you abandon the law of Christ and follow Jewish customs?" The Romans had been enlightened by the teaching of Paul, who says, "For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing." So those from the Gentiles were convinced that without Christ there is no other way to be saved, and that one must not keep the Jewish types. Paul found a fight; he finds the discord. He throws himself into the middle of the combatants and reconciles the two sides. And consider: first of all, Paul did not demand strict exactness from everyone, but had in mind what was safe. For prejudice is hard to undo, and habit is barely erased by time. He did not want, by forcing the Jews to eat foods, to turn them away from the faith; rather, he wanted first for faith in Christ to take root in them. What, then, of those who had become Christians from among the Jews? When they saw themselves being exposed as not yet having believed in Christ, since they observed Jewish food laws and wanted to abstain from pork, wishing to cover up their weakness, they pretended not to eat meat at all, and ate vegetables, so that by not eating meat at all the evidence of their old habit would be hidden. Paul enters, settles the fight, and shows who thinks rightly and who is weak, and says: "Brothers, one person believes he may eat anything," as a Christian, as a believer, "while the weak person eats vegetables." "One person believes he may eat anything," knowing that all things are made clean by faith. "For everything God created is good," says the Apostle, "and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God." "The weak person": he calls it weakness to still follow Jewish custom. "The weak person eats vegetables." Many have thought these words were spoken about ascetics and about those who eat without distinction. But the holy tongue would never have slipped into such an absurd line of argument as to call the ascetics weak and those who eat everything believers. Rather, he says it to distinguish those who refuse Jewish foods from the indifference of those who partake of everything without discrimination: "One person believes he may eat anything," as a Christian, "while the weak person eats vegetables." Yet he calms the fight. He showed the difference, that the one is a matter of faith and the other of weakness. And once he had exposed it, he brought them together in friendship: "But let not the one who abstains judge the one who eats," that is, let the one from the Jews not judge the one from the Greeks for eating contrary to the law of Moses. "And let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains." For they despised them: "You have not become Christians; you have not yet believed." "Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, for God has accepted him. Who are you to judge another's servant?" See the wonder of it: how in the same words he both silences the fight and shows the Jews that they need correction. "Who are you to judge another's servant?" He says this to the Christian from the Gentiles: "Who are you to judge another's servant?" He calls him "another's" because he seemed to be under the law. "To his own master he stands or falls; and he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand." So too of the Judaizers: "And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand." He ended the fight and brings peace back in: so, "Who are you to judge another's servant? To his own master he stands or falls; and he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand." So "one person esteems one day above another, while another esteems every day alike." What does "one person esteems one day above another" mean? Since even among the Judaizers some abstained from foods entirely, say from pork, while others honored only the Sabbath, on set days, he says, "One person esteems one day above another, while another esteems every day alike." Then: "The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord, and the one who does not observe the day does not observe it for the Lord. And the one who eats eats for the Lord, and the one who abstains abstains for the Lord." See how he ends the fight. "Who are you to judge another's servant?" So let not the one who abstains judge the one who eats, and let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains. "For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ." Pay attention here: "By myself I swear that to me every knee shall bow." So he calms the fight between the combatants. He says, "Who are you to judge another's servant? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ." Where does this come from? "For it is written: As I live, says the Lord, to me every knee shall bow." So: "Why do you judge your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. For it is written: As I live, says the Lord, to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall confess the true God." In answer to this it has been said: if after the cross he received worship as a reward, how did the prophets proclaim his worship before the cross? But let this suffice, so that our father's teaching may also set its seal on our thought, and let us all together send up glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
